channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: New Digital Collections Now Available
item.description: Tulane University Libraries: “Digital Initiatives has recently added three new collections to the Tulane University Digital Collections (TUDC), expanding access to materials documenting Louisiana history, Central American political history, and New Orleans music.”

item.title: Biddeford library to archive memorial items honoring ICE shooting victim
item.description: Portland Press Herald: “Since [Sebastián] Durán Guerrero’s death on July 13, community members have left cards, flowers, notes, art and other items at two memorial sites. Archiving those items will preserve an important part of Biddeford history, the library said. Archivist and reference librarian Rose Dionne said Durán Guerrero’s death was a ‘huge event’ that happened in Biddeford, and it’s important to memorialize it.”

item.title: Science Museum ends BP sponsorship after 25 years
item.description: Museums Association: “The Science Museum and BP have ended their commercial relationship, following years of high-profile protests by environmental groups. In a statement, the chief executive of the Science Museum Group (SMG), Ian Blatchford, said its partnership with the company had “drawn to a close” at the end of the current contract term, which was Monday 31 August. The SMG did not give a reason as to why the contract has not been renewed.”

item.title: British-Nigerian influencer dies after penis enlargement injection in Bangkok ‘triggered fatal embolism’
item.description: Malay Mail: ” A British-Nigerian influencer died after a penis enlargement procedure in Thailand allegedly triggered a fatal pulmonary embolism, according to a UK coroner’s report cited by the New York Post. Igho ‘Tiny’ Ubiribo, 43, was on holiday in Bangkok with his wife, Daniella Simba Allen, when he underwent the cosmetic procedure on March 5.”

item.title: Seattle Times, Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over AI training
item.description: Investing.com: “The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleges the companies scraped content from the newspapers’ websites, including articles behind paywalls, and incorporated the material into datasets used to train and operate AI products.”

item.title: ‘Reasonable’ consumers know they don’t own digital downloads, Sony says
item.description: Engadget: “As PlayStation players prepare for an all-digital future after January 2028, Sony is making no apologies to anyone confused about what that means for game ownership (or lack of it). In fact, the company has told a Californian court that no ‘reasonable’ consumer would be silly enough to think that purchasing a game digitally means that it actually belongs to you.”

item.title: Track NASA’s Roman Space Telescope on its long cruise to deep space
item.description: Mashable: “As the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope heads for deep space, the public can follow its three‑month trip in near-real time with NASA’s online tracker. The spacecraft launched on Sunday, Aug. 30, from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. It’s now cruising on its own toward its final orbit about 1 million miles away from Earth.”

item.title: Indonesia, Suriname explore cooperation on shared Javanese heritage
item.description: Antara: “Indonesia’s Culture Ministry is exploring cultural cooperation with Suriname to promote national heritage globally, drawing on the shared Javanese heritage of the two countries.”

item.title: The Wild Center commits to net zero emissions, a first of its kind
item.description: Adirondack Explorer: “The Wild Center has become the first cultural institution in the world to commit to achieving net zero carbon emissions. In collaboration with Global Network for Zero, the Tupper Lake natural history museum moved to align its climate-centered values with its actions and outputs.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New National Air and Space Museum Video Series Brings Aerospace Learning Into Classrooms
item.description: Smithsonian: “Each month of the school year, the museum will release a collection of videos focused on a specific topic. Every collection contains four videos under 10 minutes in length and an accompanying educator guide featuring classroom resources, student activities and full lesson plans. The topics for the 2026–2027 school year are weather (September), the solar system (October), art (November), air ships (February), moons (March) and comets and meteors (April).”

item.title: New Twitter rebrands to Tweet.app after court’s double-edged ruling
item.description: Engadget: “The Tweet.app website is currently live, but is still only accepting waitlist applicants for its upcoming social media platform. According to TechCrunch, more than 172,000 have already signed up and requested a handle, which costs $20 to reserve.”

item.title: I stopped memorizing Linux commands and started playing this instead
item.description: MakeUseOf: “There are plenty of Linux terminal commands that can make the shell feel less intimidating, but memorizing them from a list has never worked especially well for me. GameShell gives all of that syntax a place to stick. Instead of memorizing commands in a vacuum, I was climbing a castle tower, building a hut, clearing spiders out of a cellar, and shuffling coins around with the same commands I’d use in a normal shell.”

item.title: White House launches Arcade.gov with computer game that lets players ‘deport’ migrants
item.description: ABC News: “The White House announced the launch of what it called “Arcade.gov,” a website of five versions of classic computer games promoting the president’s agenda. The games include ‘Flappy Bill,’ ‘Build the Wall,’ ‘Rio Run,’ ‘Supply Line’ and ‘Trump Savings Tycoon.’ One of the games, ‘Rio Run,’ a variation on the popular Snake computer game, has players “deport” migrants along the Rio Grande along the U.S.-Mexico border.”

item.title: Elon Musk is beefing with…an online chess site?
item.description: Business Insider: “Musk’s companies have yet to conquer the chess world. In a 2025 chess battle, xAI’s Grok 4 reached the final round but was bested by OpenAI’s o3 model. He hasn’t always been so loving of the game. In 2012, he shut down a chess tournament among Tesla employees. ‘Indeed, we do not have time for chess,’ Musk told Business Insider at the time.”

item.title: Once popular for attacking AI, ASCII smuggling is embraced by spammers
item.description: Ars Technica: “A clever technique used to hide malicious prompts in attacks on AI agents has been adopted by spammers to evade filters on email platforms that are designed to flag unwanted messages used in mass campaigns.”

item.title: US military turns off ad trackers on devices amid Middle East targeting reports
item.description: Reuters: “U.S. military officials say they have disabled advertising trackers on a ​range of phones and computers, according to letters released on Friday by U.S. Senator Ron Wyden and statements given ‌to Reuters, a development that follows reports that commercially available location data had been used to target American forces in the Middle East.”

item.title: New IRS proposal threatens universities’ tax-exempt status over diversity programs
item.description: Politico: “The Trump administration unveiled a plan Thursday to cancel the tax-exempt status of universities that it says give preferential treatment to minority students. The proposed regulations released by the IRS are aimed at preventing discrimination on the basis of race and could affect up to 18,000 high schools, universities and trade schools, the agency said.”

item.title: Africa’s mother tongues are finding new life as youth connect with roots and relatives
item.description: Associated Press: “Africa is home to over 1 billion people speaking roughly a third of the world’s languages, with between 1,500 and 3,000 across 54 countries, according to UNESCO. Experts say the revival in some of them is driven partly by second- and third-generation Africans in the diaspora finding it easier to reconnect with their roots and communicate with older relatives, thanks to social media, online learning and entertainment.”

item.title: Has Academic Twitter found its voice again?
item.description: Times Higher Education: “The migration to Bluesky, LinkedIn and Mastodon, which accelerated with the re-election of Donald Trump in November 2024, was assumed by many to be the end of the community known as Academic Twitter. Yet the issues raised by the [Jason] Arday case has reignited debates on the platform in a way not seen for several years.”

item.title: How Gold Plastic Syndrome Is Killing Toys And Game Consoles
item.description: Hackaday: “In a recent video [Sqwerks] does a deep-dive into the problem of disintegrating plastic enclosures of Nintendo DS consoles. These original NDS handheld consoles have a metallic-like coating that appears to interact with the ABS plastic, causing yellowing as well as extreme brittleness and correspondingly broken hinges. Unsurprisingly, this causes the shell to essentially disintegrate the moment you try to disassemble them for something like a screen replacement.”

item.title: Text Adventures Are Still Doing Alright
item.description: The Virtual Moose: “Even though the general narrative online seems to be that text adventures died with Infocom (which I disagree with for many reasons of course), it’s nice to see that there’s two notable Interactive Fiction and Text Adventure events happening at the same time. The first is that the 32nd Annual IF Comp is now live! There are 71 new interactive fiction entries to play and vote on. Not all of them are pure text adventures but the entries let you know what type of Interactive Fiction it is.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Redditors say Anthropic’s expensive Claude plans offer far less usage than advertised
item.description: Mashable: “A popular Reddit post in r/Anthropic titled ‘More Drama’ has drawn significant attention this week, amplifying claims that Anthropic has been misleading customers about how much usage they actually get with its higher-priced Claude subscription plans.”

item.title: How a donkey named Eloise became a symbol in the fight against Florida data centers
item.description: Miami Herald: “As Florida’s summer of data center backlash has worn on, residents fighting the warehouses have found reasons for hope. Fierce public pushback has halted not just the Citrus County proposal, but others in Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties. Political pressure has grown for candidates running in Florida elections to lay out clear positions on data centers. And residents have banded together with the power of clipboard petitions, homemade T-shirts and Facebook groups. Out of this environment, local symbols of resistance have been born. Symbols like Eloise.”

item.title: Meta’s data center will be the biggest in the U.S., but no one knows who they’re hiring
item.description: The Lens: “Research shows that AI data center facilities are landing in Black and low-income communities already treated as environmental sacrifice zones. In Louisiana, the two neighboring towns have a majority Black population, but residents fear that the jobs are not reaching them.”

item.title: Kris Mayes calls for no new AI data centers as Arizona faces water, power crunch
item.description: Arizona Mirror: “Arizona Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes is calling for a statewide pause on new data centers, specifically those aimed at powering artificial intelligence systems, amid rising energy costs and the federal government’s plan to cut 30% of Arizona’s Colorado River supply.”

item.title: Entergy blows a fuse over mistakenly shared documents revealing who’s paying data center bills
item.description: Arkansas Times: “Explosive revelations in the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette today show that Google, the Silicon Valley giant building data centers in Little Rock and West Memphis, will pay only about a third of the price tag of its 600-megawatt solar facility in Jefferson County. The documents also reveal the full power draw of its 1,100-acre West Memphis project for the first time.”

item.title: Kenyans Did College Students’ Homework for Years. Then A.I. Arrived.
item.description: New York Times: “Mr. Bundi estimates he wrote more than 2,500 essays over the next 12 years, sometimes three a day. He balanced completing his public health degree with helping faraway students studying engineering, medicine and computer science to finish theirs. Some students gave him their school login information so he could keep up with their assignments. Mr. Bundi didn’t know it then, but he was in the boom era of internet gig work.”

item.title: UMW Launches Virginia’s First Master’s Degree in AI in Business
item.description: University of Mary Washington: “The University of Mary Washington has opened enrollment for a new Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence in Business (MS in AI in Business), an innovative graduate program designed to prepare professionals for a rapidly evolving, AI-driven economy. The graduate degree is the first of its kind in Virginia to focus specifically on artificial intelligence in a business context, combining advanced AI technologies with the strategic, ethical and leadership skills needed to translate those tools into real-world organizational impact.”

item.title: Princeton strengthens its support for AI and data science scholarship through Data and Intelligent Systems initiative
item.description: Princeton University: “Princeton has established a new academic unit, Data and Intelligent Systems (DaIS), to help accelerate the pace of discovery in artificial intelligence and data science and to support transformative research and teaching across disciplines.”

item.title: Wisconsin congressman violates ‘spirit’ of state law regulating AI in campaigns
item.description: Spectrum News: “In the days leading up to and immediately following the Wisconsin primary election, Republican Congressman Derrick Van Orden, R-Prairie du Chien, posted deepfake videos of Rebecca Cooke, the Democrat he will face in the November election. Both are vying for the seat to represent western and central Wisconsin. The AI-generated videos make it look like Democrat Rebecca Cooke said things she didn’t.”

item.title: Chinese businesses are giving away AI tokens with coffee, credit cards, and dumplings
item.description: Rest of World: “Banks, cafes, and telcos, among other small and big businesses, are offering free AI tokens as incentives to attract more customers. Some businesses are selling tokens much like mobile data plans, offering them as credit card rewards, or giving them out like free Wi-Fi. An AI token is essentially a unit of computing that an AI model uses to process text.”

item.title: Pocket’s AI made my game ideas real. Now Meta controls the results.
item.description: Ars Technica: “After playing around with Pocket for the better part of a week, I found myself getting hooked on the simple process of quickly standing up functional, relatively feature-rich game prototypes simply by chatting with an LLM. But the result of all that time and AI effort is a couple of interactive toys that are effectively trapped in Meta’s new walled garden, without any real way to turn them into something separate.”

item.title: Judge weighing whether to block Arkansas news outlets from publishing data center pact details
item.description: Arkansas Advocate: “A federal judge is considering whether to block the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette and Arkansas Times from publishing details of an agreement regarding a West Memphis data center, a move that free speech advocates say would violate the First Amendment.”

item.title: Russia wants to sell ‘sovereign AI’ abroad. Here’s what it’s really selling.
item.description: Atlantic Council: “While Russia’s AI ecosystem lags behind those of the United States and China, Moscow can pitch its systems as giving governments more latitude to shape outputs around local information and government-defined political preferences—and less reliance on Western tech companies. The key issue is what kind of sovereignty Russia’s customers will actually get. A related question is whether authoritarian buyers might use these systems to further political repression.”

item.title: A UVA nutrition expert tested AI diet-tracking apps. Here’s what she found
item.description: University of Virginia: “A registered dietician, [Professor Sibylle] Kranz signed up for free trials of several popular apps, creating different user profiles and health goals to test features and compare advice. The results proved to be a mixed bag of convenience and possible inaccuracies.”

item.title: UNC Awarded Up to $35 Million to Lead Landmark Initiative to Build World’s Largest Data Resource for Rare Disease AI
item.description: UNC Healthcare: “To address the challenges of rare disease diagnosis, the UNC School of Medicine and Emory University are leading a first-of-its-kind research initiative to build a comprehensive data resource. Designed to power AI-driven insights, new and existing tools will enable analysis of these large-scale clinical and biological data to help rare disease experts make earlier diagnoses, better inform medical care, and accelerate treatment discovery.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: SPLC Unveils Database Examining In-Custody Deaths in Mississippi Jails
item.description: Southern Poverty Law Center: “The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) released a new database today tracking in-custody deaths in jails across Mississippi.”

item.title: Retake the Lake
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: a Chrome extension called (This link goes to a GitHub repository. Here is the extension in the Chrome Web store.) “This is a (hopefully temporary) extension for Chrome browsers that corrects ‘Lake America’ to ‘Lake Ontario’ in two ways.”

item.title: Judge blocks X rival from using Twitter name, but allows ‘Tweet’ for now
item.description: TechCrunch: “The story of the Virginia-based startup isn’t really about building something unique; it’s about a company trying to get its hands on abandoned trademarks that X relinquished. Even the homepage for the company clearly states its purpose is to go back and pick up what Elon Musk dropped when he renamed the town square as X, and ‘threw the bird away on his way out,’ it says.”

item.title: YouTube Travel Creator Drew Binsky Inks Netfix Deal
item.description: Variety: “Beginning Sept. 19, Netflix subscribers can watch a curated collection of episodes from Binsky’s content library, including his latest episode ‘Entering The World’s Narrowest Island (100 Feet Wide).’ Going forward, Binsky will release new episodes day-and-date on Netflix alongside YouTube and other platforms.”

item.title: Lush launches campaign highlighting harm caused by social media
item.description: Retail Gazette: “Lush is looking to spotlight the harm caused by big social media platforms in its new campaign, which is now live across all of its stores in the UK, EU, USA and Canada. The retailer left the major social media platforms, Snapchat, X, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook almost five years ago. And since then, the platforms have been accused of creating their platforms to be addictive by design.”

item.title: Pentagon Purges Decades of Classified Documents After WaPo Revealed Top Brass Warned Hegseth
item.description: Mediaite: “The Pentagon reportedly removed decades’ worth of classified military documents from a secret network used by defense officials and U.S. troops after The Washington Post revealed that several top military leaders had raised concerns about extending the war with Iran.”

item.title: Opera loses court challenge against EU exemption of Microsoft’s Edge from DMA rules
item.description: Reuters: “Norwegian browser maker Opera on Wednesday lost its ​court challenge against EU antitrust regulators’ decision to ‌exempt Microsoft’s browser Edge from rules reining in the power of Big Tech.”

item.title: Mapping the Forest
item.description: Wake Forest University: “It took one drone, 300 million laser data points and seven teams of students on foot to map Wake Forest University’s trees. Led by Ovidiu Csillik, an assistant professor of remote sensing in the environment and sustainability studies program, the project produced a publicly accessible, interactive 3D digital map of more than 1,000 trees and helped the University earn international accreditation as a Level II arboretum.”

item.title: Facebook Groups Are Google’s No. 2 Forum Source
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “A recent analysis by Ahrefs shows that public Facebook Groups are now the second most common site in Google’s Discussions and forums module, after Reddit. Facebook appears in 38.3% of the search results where the module shows up, with all Facebook URLs coming from public Groups.”

item.title: Planting crops in fields of solar panels is more efficient, protects the plants and helps keep workers cool, study finds
item.description: LiveScience: “Compared to tomatoes grown in an open field, tomatoes grown under solar panels experienced leaf temperatures that were 1.84°C cooler during the day overall and up to 7.56°C cooler during peak afternoon heat, reducing water loss through evapotranspiration by 22.4%. Even though the simulated crops received 47% less sunlight, their carbon uptake declined by only 31%, suggesting that more temperate conditions lowered heat stress and partially offset the effects of increased shade.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Transforming the Mission: The Soviet Military’s Reorientation to a Defensive Posture in Europe
item.description: National Security Archive: “These newly available records shed light on Politburo discussions about military reform during the Gorbachev era, CIA assessments of changes in Soviet military posture in Europe, and the visit by Soviet Defense Minister Dmitry Yazov to the United States in 1989.”

item.title: The best of IFA 2026: exoskeletons, ultralight laptops, and weird new tech
item.description: MakeUseOf: “The Internationale Funkausstellung Berlin (IFA) is the world’s biggest tech show (yes, bigger than CES), and each year, it wows us with the latest and greatest in tech, with this year’s edition no different. From incredible dual-use laptops to cutting-edge AI note-taking and all the way back around to fully robotic exoskeletons for everyday use, we’ve seen it all — and this is the tech receiving one of our coveted MUO Best in Show awards this time out.”

item.title: SafeSport Sees Big Jump in Visitors to Banned Database After Announcing Sanctions Publicly
item.description: Associated Press: “The U.S. Center for SafeSport more than doubled the number of new visitors to its online Centralized Disciplinary Database in the month after it started making public announcements about people placed on its banned list.”

item.title: Nazi-looted painting must be returned to Jewish art dealer’s heir, Argentina court rules
item.description: The Guardian: “Argentina must return to the rightful owner’s heir an 18th-century painting stolen by Nazis from a Dutch Jewish art collector, a judge has ruled. Portrait of a Lady by Italian baroque painter Giuseppe Ghislandi was missing for eight decades before being photographed in 2025 hanging in the home of the daughter of a senior Nazi officer who had fled to Argentina after the second world war.”

item.title: 10 Video Downloading Hacks Every YouTube User Should Know
item.description: Lifehacker: “YouTube constantly changes its website and apps, so these methods may not always work, but I’ve tested all of them and confirmed they are working at the time of writing. It’s also important to note that downloading YouTube videos outside of the app’s official channels is against the company’s terms of service. That said, if you’re only downloading videos for personal use, you’ll likely be fine, but if you plan to reupload that content to your own YouTube channels, or attempt to monetize the content you’ve downloaded, that’s another story. Please download responsibly.”

item.title: TikTok is the new 311: New Yorkers tag Mayor Mamdani on social media for help
item.description: Gothamist: “Mamdani is being inundated with online requests for IRL fixes. The videos, which have become a meme on TikTok, show people begging Mamdani to take action on everything from mundane nuisances — like potholes and leaky subway stations — to more existential challenges like finding love. The requests have become so popular that the mayor of Los Angeles has embraced the trend, as have users everywhere from Manila to London.”

item.title: In first major ufology acquisition, Huntington puts Integratron’s eccentric history on display
item.description: Los Angeles Times: “The collection, announced by the museum Tuesday, is deep and vast, with materials dating from the 1910s through the 1990s. It includes an architectural model and original blueprints of the Integratron, as well as nearly 630 photographs, negatives and slides, more than 250 audio recordings, 8-millimeter film footage, books, publications and other records and ephemera.”

item.title: ‘It seemed like every town in America had something going on’: Week of Action against Flock and ALPRs gets people engaged
item.description: ACPC: “[Len] Phillips said the man was an example of how the event’s 110 or so attendees included people of differing political ideologies—including Democratic Socialists, Libertarians and conservatives—who nonetheless shared concerns about the proliferation of police surveillance in their communities. The same thing was seen in many of the week’s 485 events across the country, said Ed Vogel, a member of DeFlock, a national group that organized the week.”

item.title: UNICEF estimates 20 million children suffered online sexual abuse in one year
item.description: Reuters: “About 20 million internet-using children across ​21 countries were subjected to sexual exploitation or abuse on digital platforms in a single year, with most cases occurring ‌on social media platforms, a new report by the U.N. children’s charity said on Thursday. More than one in five children aged 12 to 17 across Africa, Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe experienced at least one form of sexual abuse or exploitation on online platforms in the year before being surveyed, the UNICEF report estimated.”

item.title: Your digital footprint is worth looking back on
item.description: Michigan Daily: “Think of the last time you had a Snapchat memory flashback pop up as a notification or scrolled through your Instagram archived posts. Usually, there’s an instant flash of embarrassment that often makes us treat our past selves like something to hide or erase indefinitely. There’s a modern impulse to scrub our digital footprint, the trail we leave behind through our online activities, clean from existence. Yet, doing so erases who we once were, and it strips us of a valuable tool for understanding who we are becoming.”

item.title: Carolina and Duke to combine plant collections
item.description: University of North Carolina: “UNC-Chapel Hill and Duke University will unite their herbaria under the management of the North Carolina Botanical Garden in Chapel Hill. Herbaria are collections of preserved plant specimens that serve as irreplaceable scientific archives and enable researchers to study biodiversity, long-term climate shifts, invasive species and other changes in plant life across generations. Together the collection will comprise about 1.7 million specimens, making it the third-largest university herbarium in the country after Harvard University and the University of California, Berkeley; and the largest in the southeastern United States.”

item.title: This Web Tool Lets You Create 360-Degree Illustrations
item.description: 80LV: “JUNOTA’s Gururi Paint looks very useful for creating rough background sketches. You can draw while looking around the surrounding space, giving you a better sense of the environment. It includes basic tools like a brush, palette, fill, eyedropper, eraser, and layers, plus adjustable canvas and grid settings. The basic controls are simple: hold Space and drag to look around, and hold Z and drag to zoom. According to JUNOTA, Gururi Paint is still a work in progress, and they plan to keep improving it and adding new features over time.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: AI almost sent hazmat train barreling toward ‘catastrophe’ in Eastern WA
item.description: Spokesman-Review: “A 146-car train carrying ‘hazardous materials’ was at risk of colliding with a roadway maintenance worker in Connell, Washington, had a BNSF dispatcher not caught an issue caused by an AI system. The June 16 incident would have been a ‘public catastrophe’ for the worker, driving crew and north Franklin County community, read a Wednesday letter from the Brotherhood of Railroad Signalman to the Federal Railroad Administration. At issue was BNSF’s use of an AI-powered dispatching system called Movement Planner, said Brandon Pettit, vice general chairman of the signalman union’s BNSF general committee.”

item.title: The latest tech billboard trend? Anti-AI graffiti
item.description: San Francisco Standard: “The ad from AI customer-service company Pylon in Dogpatch is likely unintelligible to many San Franciscans. But a graffitied message that recently appeared at the bottom was unambiguous: ‘Fuck your AI billboard.’… It’s just one of at least 10 anti-AI messages that have been graffitied onto tech company advertisements around the city over the past few weeks, possibly by the same person. The exact wording of the graffiti varies, but the messages are consistent in calling out the million- and billion-dollar companies for their impact on the local economy and working class.”

item.title: Data center opponents launch write-in campaigns in Billings state Senate district
item.description: Montana Free Press: “Sen. Daniel Zolnikov, R-Billings, is being campaigned against online and IRL by write-in candidates Cari Olson and Elijah Tidswell. The lawmaker’s last registered employer is Broad Reach Power, whose parent company, Houston, Texas-based EnCap Investments, is a stakeholder in Quantica Infrastructure, developer of a proposed data center near Broadview.”

item.title: Warnock calls for data center moratorium in Georgia
item.description: The Current Georgia: “U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock on Friday called for a moratorium on data center construction in Georgia, describing the secrecy surrounding plans to build a $20 billion data center in Effingham County ‘unacceptable.'”

item.title: OpenAI releasing major upgrade to ChatGPT and Codex with GPT-6 Astra, details here
item.description: 9to5 Mac: “OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra a ‘significant jump in cyber capabilities,’ adding that it ‘meets the Critical threshold⁠ in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework.’ For that reason, the model is rolling out slowly to users.”

item.title: Invasion of the Robot Teachers
item.description: Reason: “In New Mexico, Facebook and Instagram are considered a ‘public nuisance,’ but letting artificial intelligence systems record and store young kids’ voices and score their reading prowess is state policy. Starting last school year, the state required all public schools to use Amira—a personified AI system designed to assess and instruct elementary school students—for mandatory literacy assessments, dyslexia screenings, and weekly tutoring sessions in kindergarten through second grade.”

item.title: Republicans struggle for footing on data center response ahead of midterms
item.description: Politico: “The desire for action on data centers, which had already divided the House GOP conference, came up in multiple member discussions early this week — including a conversation that House Speaker Mike Johnson hosted Monday with freshman lawmakers, Republicans told POLITICO.”

item.title: More than 68% of voters support recall of Independence Councilman John Perkins
item.description: KMBC: “Voters in Independence have successfully recalled a councilman after his vote to approve a multibillion-dollar data center. District 1 Councilman John Perkins was recalled during a special election on Tuesday, with unofficial final results showing over 68 percent of voters in the district supported the recall

item.title: Prince estate respond to fans’ concern over rumours of AI use on new ‘Timeless’ release
item.description: NME: “Now, following tracks ‘With This Tear’ and ‘Stone’ being released ahead of the full album arriving on August 28, Prince’s estate have responded to rumours from fans that AI was used to complete the album, particularly on one song called ‘Calabama’.”

item.title: CNBC Accidentally Admits Why Employers Love AI
item.description: Gizmodo: “Why do employers love AI? The official story is that it increases productivity, an assertion that has yet to be proven true. But a financial expert on CNBC spoke candidly on Friday about how the rate of wage growth has plummeted this year. And he pointed to the fear workers have of asking for a raise when they could be replaced with AI.”

item.title: Bill Simmons’s Podcast Co-Hosts Are Tired of His A.I. Antics
item.description: New York Times: “Film buffs are complaining about several instances in which Mr. Simmons used ChatGPT — which he sometimes accidentally mispronounces ‘ChatGBT’ — to approximate the opinions of the deceased film critic Roger Ebert in his movie podcast, ‘The Rewatchables.’ Some argued that it was disrespectful of Mr. Ebert; others said it was incongruous that Mr. Simmons, a columnist, would use technology to misappropriate another writer’s work. Ads from OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, have run on the show this year.”

item.title: South Korea’s AI rally is reshaping romance, reality shows and academic preferences
item.description: CNBC: “South Korea’s AI stock rally is rapidly transforming different corners of the country’s society ranging all the way from romance to academics. In Korea’s dating scene, professionals such as physicians, lawyers and judges, have traditionally been the most sought-after. Now the preferences are changing, as the AI boom makes those working in the chip sector — flush with hefty bonuses — the new gems of the dating pool.”

item.title: DC court faults lawyers for Deutsche Bank subsidiary over AI hallucination
item.description: Reuters: “The District of Columbia Court of Appeals said in a ruling on Thursday that lawyers for a Deutsche Bank subsidiary in a mortgage foreclosure lawsuit cited nonexistent cases generated by artificial ​intelligence, calling the matter a ‘cautionary tale’ about lawyers’ misuse of AI.”

item.title: Researcher shows how Claude Code can be tricked simply by asking it to summarize a website
item.description: The Register: “Anthropic’s Claude Code running Opus 5 in Auto Mode can be tricked into executing attacker-controlled code simply by asking the coding agent to summarize a website. The attack works up to 80 percent of the time, according to prompt-injection wizard Johann Rehberger, aka wunderwuzzi.”

item.title: AI’s environmental impact per task balloons with more complexity
item.description: Bloomberg: “As artificial intelligence (AI) use shifts from simple, one-off queries to longer and more complex tasks, the added computing required results in a dramatically larger environmental footprint. The energy needed to build a web app using some models is equivalent to powering a home for 2 1/2 hours. That’s according to the results of a new analysis from Vals AI, an independent AI benchmarking company that evaluates models on real-world tasks.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: GBH Marks the 25th Anniversary of 9/11 with New PBS LearningMedia Educational Resources and Multiplatform Content
item.description: GBH: “GBH, the leading multiplatform creator of public media in the U.S., today announced a suite of educational tools and original content dedicated to marking the 25th anniversary of September 11, 2001. Anchoring the initiative is a new collection of free digital classroom resources from PBS LearningMedia, developed in partnership with the Massachusetts 9/11 Fund, that bring together archival video, firsthand accounts, and primary sources to help educators explore the events of September 11, their impact on individuals and communities, and their broader historical context and legacy.”

item.title: National Geographic Commemorates 25th Anniversary Of 9/11 With The Launch Of A Groundbreaking Interactive Video Archive Featuring Never-before-seen Footage And Eyewitness Testimony
item.description: National Geographic: “Today, National Geographic published a landmark, interactive video archive that allows audiences to explore never-before-seen footage and eyewitness testimony from the events of Sept. 11, 2001, drawn from its catalog of 9/11 documentaries.”

item.title: Google Maps routing trucks over Swartberg Pass sparks concern
item.description: Die Hoorn: “Concerns have been raised that Google Maps is directing trucks and other heavy vehicles over the Swartberg Pass, despite the route being unsuitable for such traffic. The issue has become increasingly relevant while Meiringspoort remains closed, with more motorists and transport operators making use of alternative routes through the region.”

item.title: Disabled Marine veteran forced to sell rare 1,000-letter WWII archive to save his family
item.description: ABC 15: “A disabled Marine Corps veteran who spent more than a decade preserving a rare collection of over 1,000 World War II letters says he now has no choice but to sell it. Joseph ‘Joe’ Alosi, 100% service-connected disabled, says mounting medical bills, the loss of his home, and family crises have left him no other option than to part with the archive he once vowed to keep intact forever.”

item.title: TikTok housing scams hit international students in the Netherlands
item.description: I Am Expat: “Fraudsters are increasingly using TikTok and social media to target students in the Netherlands with fake room listings amid the ongoing housing shortage. International students arriving for the new academic year are particularly vulnerable as tight deadlines leave many desperate for accommodation.”

item.title: 3 arrested for making fake currency after learning it from YouTube tutorials
item.description: India Today: “Hyderabad police arrested three men accused of printing and circulating fake currency after tracing their operation. Investigators said the case showed how social media tutorials and basic equipment were allegedly used to mimic genuine notes.”

item.title: Trump administration scrubs data on gender-based bullying from school civil rights survey
item.description: Associated Press: “The numbers come from the Education Department’s Civil Rights Data Collection, a federal survey of nearly every public school in the nation. The release this week covers the 2023-2024 school year, when the survey included ‘nonbinary’ as a gender category alongside male and female. However, an Associated Press analysis shows that in every column for information related to gender identity, the numbers were replaced with a code indicating ‘Suppressed in Compliance with Executive Order.’ That refers to an executive order that President Donald Trump signed on his inauguration day calling for the federal government to define sex as only male or female.”

item.title: New App Encourages Canadians to Explore Aquatic Barriers Blocking Fish Migration
item.description: Canadian Wildlife Federation: “The Canadian Wildlife Federation (CWF) is calling on all Canadians to help monitor freshwater connectivity through the new Canadian Fish Passage Assessment (CANFISHPASS) app, a free mobile tool that helps identify barriers potentially restricting fish movement in rivers, streams and other waterways.”

item.title: Common myna birds travelling on Sydney trains go viral on social media
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “You may have heard of snakes on a plane, but what about birds on a train? A pair of common myna birds have become regulars on Sydney’s inner-city North Shore Line, perching themselves on the back of the seats during quieter hours. The lively duo went viral after Sydney journalist Jackie Dent posted a recording of their morning on social media.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Boston Public Library and Harvard IDI Release Open Dataset from 135 Years of Historic Newspapers
item.description: Boston Public Library: “BPL holds tens of millions of pages of historical newspapers on microfilm, roughly three million of which have been digitized and made searchable online through DigitalCommonwealth.org. Now, BPL and the Institutional Data Initiative (IDI) at the Harvard Law School Library are releasing a new dataset drawn from more than 1.47 million scanned newspaper pages — a window into 135 years of the public record, from 1795 to 1930.”

item.title: Judge refuses to block Pentagon from firing Stars and Stripes staffers over CBS interview
item.description: Associated Press: “A federal judge refused Friday to block the Pentagon from firing three Stars and Stripes staff members who claim they were illegally disciplined for speaking out about the military news outlet’s need to maintain its editorial independence.”

item.title: Exclusive / YouTube cracks down on ‘ghost creators’
item.description: Semafor: “YouTube removed videos linked to a network of AI-supercharged ‘ghost creators’ after Semafor exposed a new online business seeking to capitalize on the platform’s advertising by churning out cheap, sensationalized political videos.”

item.title: Wikimedia Foundation Workers Overwhelmingly Vote to Form Union with CWA
item.description: Communications Workers of America: “U.S.-based workers at Wikimedia Foundation—the nonprofit organization that hosts Wikipedia and sister projects—have won their union election, voting overwhelmingly to join Communications Workers of America (CWA) Local 9415.”

item.title: Almost 50 jobs could go at National Library and Archives, PSA warns
item.description: Radio New Zealand: “A proposal to cut 12 percent of the workforce at the National Library and Archives NZ will decimate both organisations and have a significant impact on service levels, says the Public Service Association (PSA).”

item.title: Influencer boom at US Open tests boundaries of tennis etiquette
item.description: Reuters: “Celebrities have long been ubiquitous in the stands – from A-list ⁠stars to U.S. President Donald Trump – as the ultra-wealthy shell out thousands of dollars for seats at the see-and-be-seen event of New ​York’s summer sporting calendar. But the growing love affair between influencers and the premier American tennis event has caused some growing pains. A chair umpire ​was forced to reprimand a group of patrons for staging a disruptive photo shoot while two-time U.S. Open champion Naomi Osaka was serving during her first-round win against Anastasia Zakharova on Monday.”

item.title: FBI Probes Service Selling 153M+ Drivers Licenses
item.description: Krebs On Security: “A new identity theft service launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada. Based on interviews with individuals whose licenses are available for purchase on this service, it appears to be siphoning images collected by a widely-used identity verification company based in Louisiana.”

item.title: Healthcare cyberattacks hit pacemakers and millions of patient records
item.description: The Register: “Two major healthcare businesses, Boston Scientific and McKesson, disclosed more details over the weekend about separate cyberattacks that disrupted global operations and resulted in stolen patient data, respectively.”

item.title: Revealed: inside the US military’s plan to tap huge sums from the NIH
item.description: Nature: “The US National Institutes of Health (NIH) is seeking to redirect research projects worth hundreds of millions of dollars from its infectious-diseases institute to military biodefence programmes at the US Department of Defense (DOD), according to two NIH employees. They confirmed to Nature that the NIH and the DOD, also called the Department of War, have signed an agreement for the arrangement.”

item.title: It’s time for Mark Zuckerberg to resign from Meta
item.description: The Guardian: “Ushering in hope for the future of technology requires changing Meta’s leadership now, so that the future is collectively imagined and built upon a new reputation and commitment. Zuckerberg does not deserve another chance simply because he can afford it. We as a society ultimately pay for his mistakes. Now is the time for shareholders to speak up and push back on Zuckerberg’s dominance and control.”

item.title: US Forest Service closing 23 research facilities as part of reorganization under Trump
item.description: Denver Post: “The U.S. Forest Service is closing 23 research stations in more than a dozen states as part of an organizational overhaul under President Donald Trump that is intended to trim costs and concentrate the agency’s resources in Western states, officials said Thursday.”

item.title: Cockroaches producing energy-rich milk bag this year’s chemistry Ig Nobel prize as ceremony leaves ‘unsafe’ US
item.description: Chemistry World: “The 36th Ig Nobel prize ceremony – which celebrates research that ‘makes people laugh, then think’ – saw an international team of researchers take home the chemistry prize last night for finding that milk-producing cockroaches are more efficient than cows.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: LaScala TV for free
item.description: Limelight: “Milan’s Teatro alla Scala has removed the paywall from its streaming platform LaScalaTV, giving audiences worldwide free access to a growing archive of opera, ballet and concert performances. From September 1, the platform is available free of charge after registration, replacing the subscription model introduced when LaScalaTV launched in 2023.”

item.title: Google escapes ad tech breakup in third Big Tech antitrust loss for US
item.description: Reuters: “U.S. Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, declined to make Google sell AdX, where publishers pay Google a 20% fee to sell ads in auctions that happen instantly when users load websites. The Department of Justice had argued Google could not be trusted to run the online advertising exchange after Brinkema ruled that Google had illegally ​quashed competition.”

item.title: Colombia’s armed groups turn TikTok and Facebook into recruiting grounds for children
item.description: The City Paper: “Human Rights Watch has warned that illegal armed groups are increasingly using TikTok, Facebook and other social-media platforms to recruit children, combining propaganda, promises of money and status, coded language and carefully chosen emojis to draw minors toward illegal armed organizations.”

item.title: MrBeast will try to survive ‘the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes’ using Gemini and Fitbit Air in deal with Google
item.description: 9to5 Google: “In a ‘multi-year partnership’ that extends beyond YouTube, Google will work with MrBeast – aka Jimmy Donaldson – to promote Gemini and Google Health. This starts with a video going live on September 5 on the MrBeast channel that will see Jimmy and co racing through the jungle, desert, and the Arctic, relying on Gemini to help guide them through the challenge.”

item.title: Is Someone Hacking DoD Refrigerators?
item.description: Schneier On Security: “Each service declined to answer questions about how many bases are affected by the outages, referring all questions to the Defense Department. Pentagon officials did not respond to questions.”

item.title: A decade’s worth of Steam files totaling more than 12TB has leaked
item.description: Engadget: “A treasure trove of Steam data has been leaked, which seemingly contains everything that was published on Steam between 2003 and 2013. The leak totals more than 12TB in scale and includes beta builds and completely finished games from Valve’s own franchises, including Half-Life, Left 4 Dead and Portal.”

item.title: Healthcare cyberattacks hit pacemakers and millions of patient records
item.description: The Register: “Two major healthcare businesses, Boston Scientific and McKesson, disclosed more details over the weekend about separate cyberattacks that disrupted global operations and resulted in stolen patient data, respectively.”

item.title: In praise of the open digital classics ecosystem
item.description: Perseus Digital Library Updates: “We have an article that is about to appear in the Journal of Open Humanities Data on ‘Perseus and the Open-Source Ecosystem of Greco-Roman Studies,’ but I thought I would precede that more formal discussion with a very recent example of what you can do in this open ecosystem.”

item.title: About half of Americans say they spend too much time on their smartphone
item.description: Pew (PEW PEW PEW PEW PEW!): “Between scrolling, notifications, and messages, smartphones can be hard to put down. Just over half of U.S. adults say they spend too much time on their smartphone, according to a Pew Research Center survey from May and June 2026. About a third of adults say their smartphone use is about right, while just 3% say they spend too little time using these devices.”

item.title: A City Unites Around a Common Goal: Moving a Castle by Hand
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “The children, about 480 total working in shifts, were taking part in the ancient tradition of hikiya, which involves moving buildings with ropes and rollers rather than dismantling them. They were trying to move Hirosaki Castle’s keep — its central, most fortified part — closer to its original base. In 2015, the keep had to be moved because an earthquake damaged a stone wall underneath the structure. (Residents also helped pull the castle that time.) With the repairs recently completed, the city of Hirosaki summoned the public again to help move the castle back.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Three Mount Shasta climbers rescued after relying on AI to plan climb
item.description: KRCR: “The USFS said the climbers told them they had used an artificial intelligence platform, YouTube videos and AllTrails to plan the trip. They said they relied on AI to decide what food to bring and how much food and water they would need. The group said it packed supplies for an eight-hour climb, not its roughly 16-hour ascent. The climbers said AI recommended simple carbohydrates instead of fats because fats ‘take too long to digest.'”

item.title: A Data Center Revolt By Historic Battlefield Is Now a Blueprint for Backlash
item.description: Bloomberg: “Data center landlords bankrolled by Blackstone Inc. and Brookfield Asset Management planned a $100 billion project after promising life-changing money to property owners in Virginia’s Prince William County. Dozens of residents sold more than 1,600 acres (647 hectares) to the developers in time for the AI boom, and another 200 banded together to sell 1,900 acres for more data centers. Others — including a group of fired-up retirees from a gated senior housing estate nearby — mobilized to save the community.”

item.title: Judge refuses to block Arkansas news reporting on Google data center energy documents
item.description: CNBC: “An Arkansas federal judge on Wednesday denied a request by an energy company to temporarily block the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette from publishing additional details from confidential documents that the newspaper obtained about the company’s involvement in building a facility that will supply power to a $4 billion Google data center in that state, a court filing showed.”

item.title: A data center battle unfolds 30 miles north of Manhattan
item.description: Spectrum News: “The public backlash against data centers has become a potent political issue across the country, and one battle is playing out just 30 miles north of New York City, where residents are fighting a project that’s moving forward despite a statewide moratorium.”

item.title: Is this the future of America?
item.description: The Verge: ” Within the past few years, data centers have been elevated from an unremarkable part of daily life in Loudoun to something that many residents now think about every day. For some, it’s the constant hum they hear from their decks; for others, it’s the transmission towers that loom over their favorite green space, or the surprise call from their energy utility that one of those towers could go up in their own backyard. While residents recognize that data centers have brought a lot of prosperity to the county, they’re beginning to wonder how much more they can take.”

item.title: Silicon Valley parents are leading a backlash against tech in the classroom
item.description: San Francisco Chronicle: “Palo Alto parent Tilli Bannett is a venture capitalist who invests in tech companies, but at a recent school board meeting, she challenged district leaders to remove most tech from classrooms.”

item.title: Erika Donalds says more AI can benefit FL students, warns against overregulation
item.description: Miami Herald: “Erika Donalds, a charter school executive heavily involved in education policy whose husband, Byron Donalds, is the GOP nominee for governor, said Wednesday she thinks artificial intelligence can help Florida students and teachers thrive. In many cases, she added, AI will ‘be the best teacher’ available to students.”

item.title: Data centers bill passes Assembly days before session ends
item.description: The Sun: “Data center operators would have to submit information about their facility’s energy consumption to the state if a newly passed California bill is signed into law. Assembly Bill 1577, authored by Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, D-San Ramon, mandates that information about energy usage be sent to the California Energy Commission, as well as local government agencies that regulate permitting.”

item.title: ‘The landscape has changed dramatically’: States defy the tech lobby on AI rules
item.description: Politico: “Interviews with more than a dozen state lawmakers, tech representatives and AI regulation advocates revealed a defiant mood sweeping through statehouses. Legislators are increasingly ignoring warnings from the tech lobby and its Washington allies about an unworkable ‘patchwork’ of conflicting laws — and are instead preparing bills to address the safety of advanced models, new AI auditing standards, chatbot protections for kids and the impact of data centers.”

item.title: “I Hope They Choke On An AI-Generated Fishbone” – James Pond Creator On System 3’s “Soulless” Legacy Collection
item.description: Time Extension: “When Rogue AI was revealed, Chris Sorrell – who, in addition to creating the character, also served as the programmer, designer and artist on James Pond: Underwater Agent, James Pond 2: Codename Robocod and James Pond 3: Operation Starfish – had some choice words to give. Given that Pond is back in the news, I reached out to Sorrell for comment – and he had plenty to say.”

item.title: Clooney tells Venice festival that AI threatens film and journalism
item.description: Reuters: “U.S. actor George Clooney warned on Wednesday that advances in ​artificial intelligence were making it increasingly difficult to distinguish truth from fiction, posing a challenge ‌for journalists, governments and the public. Speaking at the Venice Film Festival, where he is receiving a Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, the actor, filmmaker and political activist said deepfake technology and AI-generated content were undermining trust in information.”

item.title: Elon Musk’s xAI used child porn to train Grok models, lawsuit says
item.description: Ars Technica: “xAI has now been accused of training Grok on child sex abuse materials (CSAM), as regulators and courts continue to probe how far the problem goes, and some Grok users have been arrested.”

item.title: Trump administration says a New York Times win in OpenAI lawsuit would “threaten national security” and hurt small newsrooms
item.description: NiemanLab: “On Wednesday, the Trump administration threw its support behind OpenAI, backing the AI giant in its ongoing litigation with The New York Times. The Department of Justice voiced its support through a statement of interest (SOI) filed with the Manhattan judge overseeing the case, which includes several other plaintiffs, including daily papers owned by Alden Global Capital, high-profile book authors, and smaller nonprofit newsrooms like The Intercept.”

item.title: Imagining the Digital Future Center reports on ‘The Rise of AI Companions’
item.description: Elon University: “A new survey finds that 27% of U.S. adult internet users have social and emotional interactions with artificial intelligence systems, with a third of those users considering their AI bot as a friend.”

item.title: HathiTrust receives grant to deliver AI-enabled access to digital books
item.description: HathiTrust: “Researchers, students, and the broader public will have new paths into the HathiTrust collection thanks to a Mellon Foundation award to develop responsible, equitable, and transparent services that leverage AI for the public good and scholarly discovery. Two respected collaborators will join HathiTrust in this effort: Northeastern University Library, which brings deep expertise in digital scholarship, and Authors Alliance, a nonprofit that supports authors who want their work to benefit the public.” Good morning, Internet…
